title: Farmers’ Perceptions of Climate Variability, Its Impacts on Green Gram Production, and Adaptation Strategies in Tharaka Nithi County, Kenya
content:
This study of smallholder households in Tharaka North, Kenya, reveals widespread perceptions of climate variability and its adverse effects on green gram production, but limited uptake of adaptation measures. The findings highlight low adaptation adoption, the dominance of soil and water conservation among adopters, and the role of socioeconomic, farm-level and gender-related factors in shaping adaptive capacity.


ABSTRACT

This study assessed farmers' perceptions of climate variability, its impacts on green gram production, and adaptation strategies in Tharaka North Sub-County, Tharaka Nithi County, Kenya. Primary data were collected from 393 green gram-producing households using a structured questionnaire administered through the Open Data Kit (ODK) mobile application. Descriptive statistics and econometric models were used to analyze farmers' perceptions and the determinants of adaptation strategy adoption. Most farmers (93.9%) perceived increasing rainfall variability and rising temperatures, which they associated with greater drought stress and declining green gram yields. Soil and water conservation (51.7%), expansion of land under green gram cultivation (23.4%), livelihood diversification (8.7%), and intercropping (8.1%) were the common adaptation strategies, although adoption was constrained by limited access to climate information, financial resources, and extension services. Adaptation decisions were significantly influenced by age, education, farming experience, farm size, non-farm entrepreneurship, and institutional support. Gender differences in adaptation choices were also evident. These findings underscore the need for strengthened climate information services, extension support, and targeted climate-smart interventions to enhance the resilience and productivity of green gram farming systems in Kenya's Arid and Semi-Arid Lands (ASALs).
